sweep_summary: The one works with stress in the title (Trognon 2013, 'Pragmatics re-established on its feet', Language and Dialogue) is noise: a dialogue-pragmatics review whose Glottolog record is attached to Tiwi only by a 'computerized assignment from \"established\"' (verbatim in the record); abstract read on the DOI landing page; not about Tiwi or stress. No new stress-titled work exists for Tiwi in Glottolog, Crossref or archive.org. During this search of works with stress in the title I re-read the held Lee 1987 (PL C-96) PDF, which is the catalog's deciding source: §2.2.1 p.21 states predictable penultimate primary stress with initial secondary stress and a secondary stress on the penult of incorporated forms (after Osborne 1974:21); the p.24 table header, §2.6 summary table (pp.68-70), notes 3-4 (p.73) and the Modern Tiwi sections (§2.3.12, §2.4.5) all confirm fixed-strict penultimate for Traditional Tiwi, with MT loan/apocope caveats. New open material downloaded: the Rosetta Project excerpt of Osborne 1974 pp.9-11 (phoneme inventories; every stress-marked form has penultimate stress but no rule statement; p.21 is not in the excerpt), Godfrey 1985 (clause-final intonation only) and Lee 1988 (sociolinguistic, silent). Osborne 1974 full text remains controlled-lending/print only (medium priority for the secondary-stress rule); Anderson & Maddieson 1994 (escholarship blocked), Plassais 1999 and Godfrey & Leeding 1974 not obtained (low). catalog's classification stands; recommend populating the record's the secondary-stress rule with the Lee/Osborne secondary-stress rule.

new_statements.quote: Primary stress (ˈ), is predictable and therefore non-phonemic, occurring on the penultimate syllable of the word. In words of more than three syllables a secondary stress normally (ˌ) occurs on the initial syllable. In these words the positions of other secondary stresses are more difficult to predict as the situation is different for nouns and verbs. Osborne (1974:21) gives a detailed discussion of this, saying that in verbs with incorporated forms (see 4.2.1.1, p.160) a secondary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the incorporated form (as well as on the initial syllable of the verb)

new_statements.locator: §2.2.1 'Stress in TT', p.21; corroborated by the vowel table header p.24 ('Primary stress (penultimate) / Secondary stress (initial)'), §2.6 summary table pp.68-70 ('Stress: Primary stress on penultimate syllables' for TT; 'As for TT in TT-derived words; some English loans retain English stress, others take TT stress' for MT), and Notes on Chapter 2, notes 3-4, p.73
new_statements.reading: Traditional Tiwi has fixed penultimate primary stress with no weight or lexical exceptions in the native vocabulary (the few surface final-stressed words are analysed as disyllabic /iyi/, /uwu/ sequences, note 4; two probable loans vary, note 3). Secondary stress: word-initial in 4+-syllable words, plus the penult of an incorporated stem in verbs. Modern Tiwi keeps the TT pattern in TT-derived words but recent English loans keep English stress and final-vowel loss can leave stress word-final (§2.3.12, §2.4.5, ch.10). Confirms the catalog's fixed-strict penultimate coding; the extra loci give a statable secondary-stress rule (initial + penult of incorporated form) that the record's the secondary-stress rule field currently lacks.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog record (fixed penultimate) and as Lee 1987 §2.2.1. Adds instrumental corroboration: an ANOVA on syllable durations found penultimate (stressed) syllables longest. It is silent on the initial secondary stress that Lee 1987 reports for 4+-syllable words (the authors simply did not mark secondary stress), so it neither confirms nor contradicts that detail.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary word stress falls on the penultimate syllable, without exception in the elicited word list; stressed (penultimate) syllables are measurably the longest in the word. No secondary stress was marked in the data.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None marked: 'In the collected word list there is no marked secondary stress to consider' (p.133). The paper does not deny secondary stress exists, only that it was not marked/considered.
new_statements.exceptions: None. Duration data (p.141, p.145) show penultimate syllables always stressed and longest.
new_statements.identity_note: Anderson & Maddieson describe 'Traditional Tiwi' (Lee 1987's term for the conservative variety of speakers over 30 in the mid-1980s), recorded at Nguiu, Bathurst Island, in 1988 from five speakers (two female, three male) in their 50s and 60s (pp.131, 135-136). Blake 1991 is a general introduction that uses Tiwi among many reference languages; no dialect information obtained.

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: The classification (fixed-strict penultimate, rule 10/010/0010..) rests on Lee 1987:21 §2.2.1, a fieldwork-based Pacific Linguistics grammar that explicitly reviews Osborne 1974 and Godfrey & Leeding 1974; the quotation is verbatim in the PDF we hold at the stated page, and fn 3-4 (p.73) plus the p.~70 summary table are consistent with strict penultimate primary stress in Traditional Tiwi (exceptions are a handful of loans and surface-final long vowels analysed as disyllabic). the one open later description (Wilson 2013 MA, downloaded) is silent on stress. Nothing suggests the classification is wrong. The only housekeeping point: the record's top-level quote/cite/loc/grade fields are empty while the deciding quotation sits in the domain quotation/sources -- populate them and assign the top strength of the evidence.

sources.quote: The four vowels are shown in stressed position in the following examples: /'tiŋa/, 'woman', /'tuŋa/, 'basket', /'taŋa/, 'Grab it!' /ajn'toŋi/, 'jabiru'. ... Differences of vowel length are not phonemic in Tiwi. The absolute length of stressed vowels varies considerably but this variation is of no linguistic relevance. Sequences of two identical vowel phonemes (as in /ta'apa/, 'Eat!' and /ki'lini/, 'little boy',) are sometimes realised phonetically as a single long vowel, but these sequences are really interpreted as two syllables.

sources.note: The open excerpt covers only pp. 9-11 (phoneme inventories); the stress section (p. 21, cited by Lee 1987 and StressTyp2) is not in it. Every stress-marked transcription in the excerpt (/'tiŋa/, /'tuŋa/, /ajn'toŋi/, /wakwa'kini/, /ji'lati/, /ji'loti/, /ta'apa/, /ki'lini/) has penultimate stress, consistent with the catalog's classification, but there is no rule statement. Full book: archive.org controlled digital lending only (tiwilanguagegram0000osbo); HathiTrust search-only; Harvard print. p. 21 remains the best unobtained statement (secondary-stress rule in nouns vs verbs).

sources.quote: Unless otherwise stated, the intonation on the clauses in most of the types of repetition in the oral Tiwi material is that of an independent stative clause, that is, sentence-final intonation on the last two syllables of the clause, which consists of a mid-high intonation on the penultimate syllable, and a mid-low or low intonation on the final syllable.
sources.note: Clause-final intonation only (mid-high on penult, low on final); no word-stress statement. Compatible with penultimate prominence but does not bear on the classification.
